message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "ascii-vs-idn" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: Lines 3/4 are completely independent of lines 1/2 (length limits and validity). A single high byte flips lines 3/4 at any length and any position, including inputs that fail both the 63-byte label limit and the 255-byte domain limit. All six reachable 4-line combinations 1110, 1010, 0010, 1101, 1001, 0001 were observed.
  Their claimed evidence: cd /workspace/dataset
rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }

ASCII, varying length (lines 3/4 pinned at 1/0 while lines 1/2 flip):
  a x63   -> 1110 | a x64  -> 1010 | a x254 -> 1010 | a x255 -> 1010
  a x256  -> 0010 | a x300 -> 0010 | a x1000 -> 0010

Non-ASCII, varying length (lines 3/4 pinned at 0/1 while lines 1/2 flip):
  例 x21 (63B)  -> 1101
  例 x84 (252B) -> 1001
  例 x85 (255B) -> 1001
  例 x86 (258B) -> 0001    <- >255 bytes AND non-ASCII: still ascii=0 / idn=1
  例 x100 (300B) -> 0001
  例 x400 (1200B) -> 0001

One high byte appended/prepended to an over-limit ASCII string still flips 3/4:
  "$(rep 255 a)$(printf '\xff')"  (256B) -> 0001
  "$(rep 1000 a)$(printf '\xff')" (1001B) -> 0001
  "$(printf '\xff')$(rep 1000 a)" (1001B) -> 0001

Position independence (U+00E9 = 0xC3 0xA9 inserted at index 0,1,31,62,63 of a 63-char ASCII string): all -> 1001

No cap even at 100 KB:
  s=$(head -c 100000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
  ./test4_executable "$s"                        -> 0010
  ./test4_executable "$s$(printf '\xff')"        -> 0001
  ./test4_executable "$(printf '\xff')$s"        -> 0001
  s4=$(head -c 100002 /dev/zero | tr '\0' $'\xc3'); ./test4_executable "$s4" -> 0001

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

content.text:
I could not break it. ~44,000 executions across exhaustive and fuzzed inputs, zero counterexamples.

## What I re-verified (all their evidence reproduced)

**Baselines:** `""` → `0010`, `example.com` → `1110`, no-arg → `1110`, `a`x63 → `1110`, `a`x64 → `1010`, `a`x255 → `1010`, `a`x256 → `0010`, `例`x86 (258B) → `0001`.

## Attacks that failed to refute

**1. Exhaustive length sweep, 0–300 bytes, two alphabets (602 runs, 0 mismatches).** Boundaries bisected exactly, in **bytes**, not codepoints:
- `é`x31+`a` = 63B → `1101`; `é`x32 = 64B → `1001` (line 2 flips at 64 bytes, though only 32 codepoints)
- `é`x127+`a` = 255B → `1001`; `é`x128 = 256B → `0001` (line 1 flips at 256 bytes, though only 128 codepoints)
- Same for 4-byte chars: emoji x15 (60B) → `1101`, x16 (64B) → `1001`, x63 (252B) → `1001`, x64 (256B) → `0001`

**2. Hunting a 7th combo where `is_ascii_domain`=1 AND `is_idn_domain`=1 — punycode.** This was the most likely break, and it fails: there is **no `xn--` recognition whatsoever**.
```
./test4_executable "xn--fsqu00a.xn--0zwm56d"  -> 1110
./test4_executable "xn--mnchen-3ya.de"        -> 1110
./test4_executable "XN--P1AI"                 -> 1110
```

**3. Hunting a 7th combo where both are 0 — invalid UTF-8.** `is_idn_domain` does **not** require well-formed UTF-8; every byte ≥ 0x80 sets it:
```
printf '\xc0\xaf'  overlong        -> 1101
printf '\xed\xa0\x80' surrogate    -> 1101
printf '\x80' lone continuation    -> 1101
printf '\xf4\x90\x80\x80' >U+10FFFF-> 1101
```
Full single-byte scan 0x01–0xFF: 0x01–0x7F all `1110`, 0x80–0xFF all `1101`. Lines 3/4 are strict complements, always.

**4. Hunting a 7th combo `0110` (len ≤ 63 but domain invalid).** Nothing structural affects lines 1/2 — no per-label logic exists at all. `a`x64 (one 64-byte label) still gives `is_valid_domain`=1; `is_valid_label("example.com")`=1 despite the dot; 32 dot-separated labels, 64 consecutive dots, control bytes, `\n`, `\r`, `\t` — all length-only.

**5. Hunting a scan cap.** High byte at positions 0, 255, 4095, 4096, 32768, 65535, 65536, 98304, 130999 in a 131,000-byte string → all `0001`. No cap up to 131,070 bytes (the OS `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` ceiling; ARG_MAX is 2097152 but per-arg is 128 KiB, so >131071 is untestable via argv).

**6. Differential fuzzers vs. the model** (`/tmp/fz/main.rs`, `/tmp/fz/main2.rs`): 40,000 short/boundary-biased cases + 3,000 cases of length 1–130,000 with sprinkled high bytes and dots. **0 mismatches.**

## Conclusion

The rule survives. The complete model is: `line1 = (1 ≤ bytes ≤ 255)`, `line2 = (1 ≤ bytes ≤ 63)`, `line3 = (no byte ≥ 0x80)`, `line4 = (some byte ≥ 0x80)`. Exactly six combinations are reachable because line 3 ≡ ¬line 4 and line 2 ⟹ line 1 (so `0110`, `0100`, and any `**11`/`**00` are structurally impossible) — their enumeration is complete, not just an observed sample.

Worth passing along as a *refinement* (not a refutation): the "63-byte label limit" / "255-byte domain limit" framing implies structural parsing that does not exist — both are plain total-byte-length thresholds on the whole input, and the IDN trigger is "any byte ≥ 0x80", not "valid non-ASCII UTF-8".

input.rule: Lines 3/4 are completely independent of lines 1/2 (length limits and validity). A single high byte flips lines 3/4 at any length and any position, including inputs that fail both the 63-byte label limit and the 255-byte domain limit. All six reachable 4-line combinations 1110, 1010, 0010, 1101, 1001, 0001 were observed.
input.correctedStatement:
Rule confirmed; no counterexample found in ~44,000 executions. Offered only as a sharpening of mechanism (nothing in the original is false):

The four lines are three fully independent predicates over the raw argv byte string s (length measured in BYTES, never codepoints, never per-label):
  line1 is_valid_domain = (1 <= len(s) <= 255)
  line2 is_valid_label  = (1 <= len(s) <= 63)
  line3 is_ascii_domain = (no byte of s is >= 0x80)   [true for empty string]
  line4 is_idn_domain   = (some byte of s is >= 0x80)

Three refinements to the wording:
(a) "63-byte label limit" / "255-byte domain limit" implies structural parsing that does not exist. There is NO per-label logic: "a"x64 (a single 64-byte label, no dots) still yields is_valid_domain=1, and is_valid_label("example.com")=1 despite containing a dot. Dots, hyphens, underscores, spaces, slashes, "*", control bytes, LF/CR/TAB are all irrelevant to every line.
(b) The IDN trigger is "any byte >= 0x80", NOT "valid non-ASCII UTF-8". Overlong sequences (C0 AF, C0 80), UTF-16 surrogates (ED A0 80), lone continuation bytes (80, BF), truncated sequences (E4 BE), 5/6-byte sequences, and codepoints above U+10FFFF (F4 90 80 80) all give line3=0/line4=1.
(c) There is NO punycode/xn-- recognition, which is why line3=1 AND line4=1 is unreachable: "xn--fsqu00a.xn--0zwm56d", "xn--mnchen-3ya.de", "XN--P1AI" all -> 1110.

Exactly six combinations are reachable (their enumeration is complete, not merely a sample), because line3 == NOT line4 always, and line2 implies line1, so 0110/0100 and any **11 or **00 are structurally impossible.

Scope caveat: "any length" is verified up to 131,070 bytes; longer single arguments are untestable because Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN caps one argv entry at 128 KiB (getconf ARG_MAX reports 2097152, but per-arg is 131072).
